notes.definition: Waves are described by their amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Wave speed is the speed at which energy is transferred through a medium, and it is given by wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f λ).
explanation: The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave away from its undisturbed (rest) position. On a diagram of a transverse wave it is measured from the middle line to a peak or to a trough, not from peak to trough. A bigger amplitude means the wave carries more energy: louder sounds and brighter light have larger amplitudes.

The wavelength (λ) is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, for example from one peak to the next peak, or from one compression to the next compression. It is measured in metres. The frequency (f) is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz); 1 Hz means one wave per second. The period (T) is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, in seconds. Period and frequency are linked by T = 1/f.

The wave speed is the speed at which energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. All waves obey the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, v = f λ, with v in m/s, f in Hz and λ in m. You must recall this equation. It can be rearranged to f = v ÷ λ or λ = v ÷ f. Remember to convert units first: kHz to Hz (× 1000), MHz to Hz (× 1 000 000) and cm to m (÷ 100).

The speed of sound in air (about 330 to 340 m/s) can be measured directly. Two people stand a measured distance apart, for example 400 m on a playing field, measured with a trundle wheel. One makes a loud sound with a visible action, such as banging two blocks together or firing a starting pistol. The other starts a stopwatch on seeing the action and stops it on hearing the sound. Speed = distance ÷ time. Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of reaction time, and using a large distance makes the time longer so the timing error is a smaller fraction of it.

Required practical 8 measures the speed of waves in a ripple tank and on a string. In the ripple tank a motor-driven dipper makes ripples and a lamp above casts their shadows onto white paper below. Measure across several waves (say 10) with a ruler and divide to find one wavelength. Find the frequency from the signal generator setting, or by counting the waves passing a point in 10 s and dividing by 10. Then use v = f λ. For a string, a vibration generator makes a standing wave on a string passing over a pulley with hanging masses. Measure the length of as many half wavelengths (loops) as possible with a metre ruler, find the wavelength, read the frequency from the signal generator and calculate v = f λ.
keyFacts: Amplitude: maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed position.
Wavelength (λ): distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave, in metres.
Frequency (f): number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
Period (T): time for one complete wave to pass a point, in seconds; T = 1/f.
Wave speed: the speed at which energy is transferred through the medium.
v = f λ must be recalled; T = 1/f is given on the equation sheet.
Speed of sound in air is about 330 to 340 m/s.
Ripple tank: measure across 10 waves and divide by 10 to find one wavelength more accurately.
Waves on a string: one wavelength equals two loops (two half wavelengths) of the standing wave.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often measure amplitude from a peak to a trough.
misconceptions.right: In fact amplitude is from the undisturbed (middle) position to a peak or to a trough. Peak to trough is twice the amplitude.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think increasing the frequency of a wave in the same medium increases its speed.
misconceptions.right: In fact the speed depends on the medium. If the frequency increases, the wavelength decreases so that v = f λ stays the same.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think wavelength is measured from a peak to the next trough.
misconceptions.right: In fact peak to trough is half a wavelength. One wavelength is from a point to the equivalent point on the next wave, such as peak to peak.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often substitute kHz or cm directly into v = f λ.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must convert to Hz and metres first to get a speed in m/s.

realWorld: Radio stations broadcast at a set frequency (for example 100 MHz); knowing the wave speed lets engineers calculate the wavelength and design aerials of the right size.
Thunder and lightning: light arrives almost instantly but sound travels at about 340 m/s, so counting the seconds between them lets you estimate the distance to a storm.
Musicians tune instruments to precise frequencies such as 440 Hz for the note A.
examTips: Write v = f λ from memory at the start of any wave speed calculation, then substitute, then calculate.
Convert kHz to Hz (× 1000) and cm to m (÷ 100) before substituting into v = f λ.
When asked how to make a wavelength measurement more accurate, say: measure across several (for example 10) waves and divide by the number of waves.
In the ripple tank, explain that the lamp makes shadows of the ripples so they can be seen and measured; a stroboscope or photograph can 'freeze' the pattern.
For the speed of sound method, name the measuring instruments (trundle wheel or tape measure, stopwatch) and say why a large distance is used.
summary: Amplitude: maximum displacement from the undisturbed position.
Wavelength: distance between equivalent points on adjacent waves.
Frequency: waves per second (Hz); period T = 1/f.
Wave speed v = f λ (recall), the speed of energy transfer.
Convert to Hz and metres before calculating.
Required practical 8: ripple tank and waves on a string, using v = f λ.

questions.question: What is the unit of frequency?
markScheme: 1 mark: Hertz (Hz)
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz; 1 Hz is one wave per second. Wavelength is in m, period in s and speed in m/s.

questions.question: Which is the correct definition of the amplitude of a wave?
options: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
The distance from a peak to the next trough
The distance from one peak to the next peak
The number of waves passing a point each second
markScheme: 1 mark: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
questions.explanation: Amplitude is measured from the undisturbed position to a peak or trough. Peak to peak is the wavelength; peak to trough is twice the amplitude (vertically) or half a wavelength (horizontally).

questions.question: Which equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
markScheme: 1 mark: v = f × λ
questions.explanation: The wave equation is v = f λ. Check with units: Hz (1/s) × m = m/s.

questions.question: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz. What is its period?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.2 s
questions.explanation: T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 s. Five waves pass each second, so each takes one fifth of a second.

questions.question: Sound waves travel through air at a constant speed. If the frequency of a sound is doubled, what happens to its wavelength?
markScheme: 1 mark: It halves
questions.explanation: The speed is fixed by the medium. From v = f λ, if f doubles then λ must halve to keep v the same.

questions.question: In the ripple tank practical, why does a student measure the length of ten waves rather than one?
options: To increase the frequency of the waves
To make the waves travel faster
Because a single wave cannot be seen
To reduce the uncertainty in the measured wavelength
markScheme: 1 mark: To reduce the uncertainty in the measured wavelength
questions.explanation: Measuring across 10 waves and dividing by 10 reduces the effect of the ruler's resolution and of the blurred edges of the shadows, so the wavelength is more accurate.

questions.question: In the ripple tank, what is the purpose of the lamp placed above the tank?
options: To cast shadows of the ripples onto paper below so they can be measured
To heat the water so the waves travel faster
To provide energy to make the ripples
To measure the frequency of the waves
markScheme: 1 mark: To cast shadows of the ripples onto paper below so they can be measured
questions.explanation: The ripples act like lenses, producing bright and dark lines (shadows) on the paper below. These make the wavelength visible and measurable.

questions.question: A standing wave on a string has 3 loops along a 1.50 m length. The vibration generator frequency is 40 Hz. What is the wave speed?
markScheme: 1 mark: 40 m/s
questions.explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength: 1.50 ÷ 3 = 0.50 m, so λ = 1.0 m. v = f λ = 40 × 1.0 = 40 m/s. Using 0.50 m as the wavelength gives 20 m/s, a common mistake.

questions.question: A student measures the speed of sound by timing a sound over a distance of 50 m with a hand-held stopwatch. Which change would most improve the accuracy of the result?
options: Use a louder sound over the same distance
Use a stopwatch reading to 0.001 s
Have the person making the sound stand closer
Use a much larger distance, such as 400 m, and repeat several times
markScheme: 1 mark: Use a much larger distance, such as 400 m, and repeat several times
questions.explanation: Human reaction time (about 0.2 s) is large compared with the 0.15 s it takes sound to travel 50 m. A larger distance gives a longer time so the reaction time error is a smaller fraction; repeats reduce random error. A more precise stopwatch does not remove reaction time.

questions.question: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 0.40 m. Calculate the wave speed.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 m/s

questions.question: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. Calculate its period.
markScheme: 1 mark: T = 1 ÷ 25
1 mark: 0.04 s

questions.question: A sound wave of frequency 2.0 kHz travels through air at 340 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2.0 kHz = 2000 Hz
1 mark: 0.17 m
questions.explanation: Convert 2.0 kHz to 2000 Hz, then λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 2000 = 0.17 m. Forgetting to convert gives 170 m.

questions.question: The period of a wave is 0.002 s. Calculate its frequency.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 Hz
questions.explanation: Rearranging T = 1/f gives f = 1/T = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 Hz.

questions.question: In a ripple tank, a student measures the distance across 10 waves as 18 cm. The frequency is 12 Hz. Calculate the speed of the ripples in m/s.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.216 m/s (allow 0.22 m/s)
questions.explanation: One wavelength is 1.8 cm = 0.018 m. v = f λ = 12 × 0.018 = 0.216 m/s.

questions.question: A standing wave on a string has 4 loops along a length of 1.20 m. The vibration generator is set to 60 Hz. Calculate the speed of the waves on the string.
markScheme: 1 mark: half wavelength = 1.20 ÷ 4 = 0.30 m
1 mark: λ = 0.60 m
questions.explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength, so λ = 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 m. v = f λ = 60 × 0.60 = 36 m/s.

questions.question: Two students stand 400 m apart. The time between seeing a starting pistol fire and hearing it is 1.2 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
markScheme: 1 mark: speed = 400 ÷ 1.2
1 mark: 333 m/s (allow 330 m/s)
questions.explanation: speed = distance ÷ time = 400 ÷ 1.2 = 333 m/s (3 s.f.).

questions.question: Sound travels through water at 1500 m/s. Calculate the frequency of a sound wave in water with a wavelength of 3.0 cm.
markScheme: 1 mark: 50 000 Hz

questions.question: A sound has a frequency of 4.0 kHz. Calculate its period in seconds.
questions.explanation: T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 4000 = 0.00025 s, which is 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ s. Using 4.0 instead of 4000 gives 0.25 s.

questions.question: Define the wavelength of a wave.
acceptedAnswers: distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave
markScheme: 1 mark: distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next / adjacent wave
questions.explanation: For example the distance from one peak to the next, or from one compression to the next.

questions.question: Define the frequency of a wave.
acceptedAnswers: number of waves passing a point each second
markScheme: 1 mark: number of waves passing a point each second (per second)
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz; 1 Hz means one wave per second.

questions.question: Describe how a student can find the frequency of the waves in a ripple tank without using the signal generator reading.
acceptedAnswers: in a measured time e.g. 10 s
markScheme: 1 mark: count the number of waves passing a fixed point in a measured time (for example 10 s)
1 mark: divide the number of waves by the time
questions.explanation: Frequency is waves per second, so count waves over a known time and divide. A longer counting time reduces the effect of timing errors.

questions.question: Explain why the wave speed found from a wave on a string uses twice the length of one loop as the wavelength.
acceptedAnswers: each loop is half a wavelength
two loops make one complete wave
markScheme: 1 mark: each loop is half a wavelength
1 mark: so one wavelength equals two loops / two times one loop
questions.explanation: A standing wave has nodes every half wavelength, so each loop between nodes is λ/2.

questions.question: State what is meant by wave speed and give its unit.
acceptedAnswers: speed at which energy is transferred
markScheme: 1 mark: speed at which energy is transferred / wave moves through the medium
1 mark: m/s
questions.explanation: Wave speed is how fast the energy moves through the medium, measured in metres per second.

questions.question: A student uses a ripple tank. Suggest two reasons why her measurement of wavelength may be inaccurate, and one improvement.
markScheme: 1 mark: the waves are moving, so lines are hard to measure / the shadow lines are blurred or have no sharp edges
1 mark: parallax or the ruler is not at the same level as the shadows
1 mark: improvement: take a photograph with a ruler in view / use a stroboscope to freeze the pattern / measure across 10 waves and divide by 10
questions.explanation: Moving, fuzzy shadows make individual wavelengths hard to measure, so freezing the image and measuring across many waves both help.

questions.question: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air using a starting pistol (or two wooden blocks), a stopwatch and a trundle wheel.
markScheme: Indicative content:
measure a large distance (e.g. 400 m) between two people using a trundle wheel
one person fires the pistol / bangs blocks, making a visible action
the other starts the stopwatch when they see the action and stops it when they hear the sound
speed = distance ÷ time
repeat several times and calculate a mean time
large distance so reaction time is a small fraction of the measured time
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear, logically ordered method including measurement of distance and time and the calculation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps but missing either a measurement or the calculation.
questions.explanation: Light arrives almost instantly, so the time between seeing and hearing is the time for sound to travel the distance. speed = distance ÷ time.

questions.question: Required practical 8. Describe how to use a ripple tank to determine the speed of water waves. Include how each measurement is made and how the result is calculated.
markScheme: Indicative content:
set up ripple tank with a small depth of water; dipper connected to a motor and power supply / signal generator
lamp above the tank, white paper or card below to show the shadows of the ripples
adjust frequency so waves are clearly visible / evenly spaced
place a ruler on the paper; measure the length across a number of waves (e.g. 10) and divide to find one wavelength
convert wavelength from cm to m
frequency from signal generator, or count waves passing a point in 10 s and divide by 10
calculate v = f × λ
repeat measurements and calculate a mean; use photograph or stroboscope to freeze the waves
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed method that would produce valid results, including how wavelength and frequency are measured and the calculation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most steps; wavelength or frequency measurement may lack detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements; not a workable method.
questions.explanation: The key is measuring wavelength across several waves with a ruler on the shadow pattern, finding frequency, and using v = f λ.

questions.question: Required practical 8. Describe how to determine the speed of waves on a stretched string using a vibration generator, signal generator, pulley, masses and metre ruler.
markScheme: Indicative content:
string attached to vibration generator, passing over pulley, with masses hanging to keep it taut
switch on and adjust the signal generator frequency until a clear standing wave (stationary loops) forms
measure the length of as many loops (half wavelengths) as possible with a metre ruler
divide by the number of loops and multiply by 2 to get the wavelength
read frequency from the signal generator
v = f × λ
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): workable method with how λ and f are obtained and the calculation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): partial method, for example only stating v = f λ or how to set up.
questions.explanation: Measuring across several loops reduces uncertainty. Remember each loop is half a wavelength.
